evidence.paraphrase: After Śukla’s meal, Vināyaka plays outside and briefly sleeps. Citizens who prepared meals seek the sage’s son at the Kāśī king’s house; the king says he left while playing. Some disparage the choice of a poor man’s inferior meal over wealthy invitations and challenge the king’s deity claim. Devotees find him sleeping at Śukla’s house: sāttvika people wait silently, while rājasika people urge him to rise before the prepared food becomes stale and criticize Śukla’s poverty. The child, explicitly called Kaśyapa’s son, says the devotional meal fully satisfied him, leaving no strength to step or appetite for another mouthful. The people become disappointed.
evidence.verifier: Krīḍā continuation5 author, direct digital body reading
evidence.verification_notes: Author witness-level Sanskrit reading checked; independent Sanskrit expert/printed-edition verification pending.

evidence.paraphrase: Seeing the citizens’ distress, the one Lord instantly becomes countless, compared to space in pots and reflected Suns. In each home he plays on stairs/swings/beds/terraces, laughs/eats with children, studies and teaches, and appears accompanied by the Kāśī king. Each householder rejoices. Oil massage, baths, footwashing, sixteen offerings, food, musk/sandal/flowers, clothing, service by wives/children/servants, sleep, Vedic recitation, song, sacred stories, Hari’s accounts, dance and lamps fill the visits. Some forms play with a noose. Purāṇa, dharmaśāstra and smṛti reading and each person’s wishes are fulfilled; Dīnanātha’s name is shown meaningful, with divine drums and flowers. The actual king cannot understand simultaneous royal/deity visits and dismisses the report before going to inspect.

evidence.paraphrase: Sanaka and Sanandana arrive after bathing, seeking food in the festive Vināyaka-filled city. In every house they see him eating, having eaten, sleeping, playing, reciting and teaching, and leave outside again. They find no pure eating place, try Śukla for hospitality, but see Kaśyapa’s son there too. Hungry and downcast, they leave the city; the divine form appears within the heart and in every direction, with eyes shut or open. After meditation they even see each other in Vināyaka’s form.

evidence.paraphrase: The all-pervading, all-formed Lord appears before the sages with TEN arms, riding a LION, with Siddhi and Buddhi. Crown, earrings, armlets, fragrance, garland, serpent, crescent, musk mark, divine clothes and radiant tusk adorn him. He is gentle to good people and difficult for wicked people to behold. The sages abandon confusion, bow and hymn eternal nondual Brahman, five elements, all forms and countless universes in his hair pores. They say he knew and fulfilled their wish and acknowledge the Kaśyapa-child manifestation for relieving the Earth’s burden. No new spoken personal request or grant follows this hymn.

evidence.paraphrase: The form disappears while they praise. Relieved of fatigue, the pair build a great temple and an image as seen, install it on an auspicious day amid sacred recitation/music and name it printed vararado’yaṃ vināyakaḥ. They name the excellent lake Gaṇeśatīrtha. Bathing, gifts and Gaṇeśa worship there remove old sin and grant all desires. Sages, gods and direction-lords arrive, worship, praise, bow and return. The chapter then says the two had come to see the child’s glory.

evidence.paraphrase: After the sages leave, the still-confused king rides from house to house seeking Vināyaka, alleging he ate alone. Residents say the deity just left with the Kāśī king; their replies intensify his exhaustion. Hearing he is at Śukla’s, he goes there and finds the child riding a bull, compared to another three-eyed deity. He bows but reproaches the child for leaving him. Vināyaka says the king ate wherever he ate, calls the accusation false and directs him to witnesses. Citizens confirm the king’s recent meal beside Vināyaka. Regaining understanding, he praises the māyā that deludes even yogins and the universally honored forms.

evidence.paraphrase: Śukla returns dejectedly with his wife, wondering whether the poor food offended the Lord. Missing the leaf hut, he becomes anxious. Servants massage, bathe and adorn both with fragrant oils, ornaments and gold garments; they behold gem/gold walls, beds/seats, pearl/gem designs, golden vessels, coverings and abundant foods. They wonder how the little dwelling became like Indra’s house. Śukla tells his wife this is Vināyaka’s grace, given unobtrusively: the Lord treats his own abundant gifts as little and a small devoted offering as great. He recommends remembering, bowing, praising and worshipping, through fear, desire, affection or even hostility, for welfare.

evidence.paraphrase: Narāntaka’s hidden envoys Śūra and Capala have waited in the city. Their roar/head movement and strength are described as terrifying even gods; they resolve to avenge earlier slain demons by killing the sage’s son in the palanquin. Taking lightning forms and roaring, they dazzle the warriors. Bearers flee, leaving Vināyaka. He seizes both in his hands and whirls them, then compassionately puts them down, saying killing a mosquito brings no manly achievement. He asks whose messengers they are and remarks that attempting one’s own power is not a fault.

evidence.paraphrase: The envoys recount earlier defeats: child-form Vighaṇṭa/Dantura burnt in an embrace; wind-form Pataṅga/Vidhula killed by head pressure; a stone-form asura printed prabala broken into a hundred pieces; donkey-form Kāma/Krodha crushed; the elephant-form name clause printed kuṇḍiyāstuvaraḥ killed by splitting the head. At Dharmadatta’s house Jṛmbhiṇī died from a coconut to the head. Jvālāsura, Vyāghratuṇḍa and Vidāraṇa attacked with city fire, wind assistance and devouring mouths and were slain. A demon explicitly named Megha, in astrologer guise, died from a ring blow. narrative_events.details: Prepared-meal invitations and disparagement of Śukla bring citizens to the sleeping child. He declares the small devotional meal satisfying and refuses another mouthful.

The one Lord becomes many, visiting every home with the king, accepting elaborate hospitality, playing/teaching and fulfilling wishes. Drums and flowers mark the event; the king cannot explain simultaneous visits.
Inspecting two or three homes, the king sees himself and the child after each meal.
Sanaka/Sanandana find the deity everywhere, cannot find a pure meal place and leave hungry. Meditation reveals Vināyaka within, around and in each other.
The ten-armed lion-mounted vision appears. The pair bow and praise, saying their wish is already fulfilled; no fresh personal grant is spoken.
After disappearance, the relieved pair install the as-seen image and name the shrine and lake. Visitors worship and depart; the sages return, followed by conditional account-hearing benefits.
The king’s exhausted house search ends at Śukla’s. His reproach meets the child’s reply and citizens’ testimony; he recognizes the deluding māyā.
Meditation brings Vināyaka-form; māyā restores royal distinction. The child is carried toward the palace in a palanquin.
Seeing the devoted couple follow, the child mentally grants extraordinary wealth without a new spoken request.
The returning couple fear offense and the missing hut, then discover servants, ornaments, palatial dwelling and food. Śukla recognizes unobtrusive grace and teaches the value of devotion.
Hidden lightning-form envoys attack. Bearers flee; the child seizes and whirls the pair, compassionately stops and questions them.
They confess Narāntaka’s mission and praise their rescuer through the five illustrative father roles.
Citizens warn of future harm. The Lord preserves his earlier fearlessness promise and releases the pair; king and child reach home.
The envoys return to Raudrapura and introduce their report with the duty to tell good and bad truthfully.
They recount the earlier demons’ forms, counters and deaths, followed by their own attack and release. Differently printed recap identities remain unresolved.
They report Śukla’s meal and simultaneous royal/deity household visits, then counsel careful self-interest and admit the child’s unmatched power.
Narāntaka rejects caution, threatens child/king and orders the four-division host to arm for Kāśī.
The equipped divisions march with frightening dust and noise; an unnamed minister rides a jeweled chariot. Gods flee to a cave as Narāntaka approaches.
